etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English belle, from Old English belle (“bell”), from Proto-Germanic *bellǭ. Cognate with West Frisian belle, bel, Dutch bel, Low German Belle, Bel, Danish bjelde, Swedish bjällra, Norwegian bjelle, Icelandic bjalla.

definitions.definition: (music) A percussive instrument made of metal or other hard material, typically but not always in the shape of an inverted cup with a flared rim, which resonates when struck.

quote.text: HEAR the sledges with the bells —Silver bells!What a world of merriment their melody foretells!

definitions.definition: An instrument that emits a ringing sound, situated on a bicycle's handlebar and used by the cyclist to warn of their presence.
The sounding of a bell as a signal.

quote.citation: 2011 December 18, Ben Dirs, “Carl Froch outclassed by dazzling Andre Ward”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: Referee Steve Smoger was an almost invisible presence in the ring as both men went at it, although he did have a word with Froch when he landed with a shot after the bell at the end of the eighth.

definitions.definition: (chiefly British, informal) A telephone call.
A signal at a school that tells the students when a class is starting or ending.
(music) The flared end of a brass or woodwind instrument.
(nautical) Any of a series of strokes on a bell (or similar), struck every half hour to indicate the time (within a four hour watch)
The flared end of a pipe, designed to mate with a narrow spigot.
(computing) The bell character.
Anything shaped like a bell, such as the cup or corolla of a flower.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: In a cowslip's bell I lie.

definitions.definition: (architecture) The part of the capital of a column included between the abacus and neck molding; also used for the naked core of nearly cylindrical shape, assumed to exist within the leafage of a capital.
(Scotland, archaic) A bubble.

quote.text: He swam to the place where Mary disappeared but there was neither boil nor gurgle on the water, nor even a bell of departing breath, to mark the place where his beloved had sunk.

definitions.definition: (British, vulgar, slang) Clipping of bell-end (“stupid or contemptible person”).
(transitive) To attach a bell to.
(transitive) To shape so that it flares out like a bell.
(slang, transitive) To telephone.

quote.citation: 2006, Dominic Lavin, Last Seen in Bangkok:
quote.text: "Vinny, you tosser, it's Keith. I thought you were back today. I'm in town. Bell us on the mobile.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To develop bells or corollas; to take the form of a bell; to blossom.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bellen, from Old English bellan (“to bellow; make a hollow noise; roar; bark; grunt”), from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to sound; roar; bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to sound; roar; bark”). Cognate with Scots bell (“to shout; speak loudly”), Dutch bellen (“to ring”), German Low German bellen (“to ring”), German bellen (“to bark”), Swedish böla (“to low; bellow; roar”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To bellow or roar.

quote.citation: 1774, Oliver Goldsmith, A History of the Earth, and Animated Nature:
quote.text: This animal is said to harbour in the place where he resides. When he cries, he is said to bell; the print of his hoof is called the slot; his tail is called the single; his excrement the fumet; his horns are called his head [...].

quote.citation: 1894 May, Rudyard Kipling, The Jungle Book, London,  New York, N.Y.: Macmillan and Co., published June 1894, →OCLC:
quote.text: As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled / Once, twice and again!

quote.citation: 1872, Robert Browning, Fifine at the Fair‎[2]:
quote.text: You acted part so well, went alɬ-fours upon earth / The live-long day, brayed, belled.

quote.citation: 1955, William Golding, The Inheritors, Faber and Faber, published 2005, page 128:
quote.text: Then, incredibly, a rutting stag belled by the trunks.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To utter in a loud manner; to thunder forth.

quote.text: Their leaders bell their bleating tunes In doleful sound.

definitions.definition: The bellow or bay of certain animals, such as a hound on the hunt or a stag in rut.
